title: Collisions of Extended Bodies in Two Dimensions
lead: When a body that is free to turn is struck, angular momentum passes into the collision along with linear momentum and energy. This section follows a disk that slides across a frictionless table and sticks to a stick nailed at one end. The force at the nail has no lever arm, so angular momentum is conserved, and working the collision through shows that the kinetic energy falls, as it must in an inelastic collision, while the linear momentum of the system actually rises. Asking where the disk would have to strike for the nail to feel no force at all leads to the percussion point, which a tennis player knows as the sweet spot of the racquet.
objectives: Observe collisions of extended bodies in two dimensions.
Examine collision at the point of percussion.
summary_html:
• Angular momentum $\kL$ is analogous to linear momentum and is given by $\kL = \kI\kw$.
  • Angular momentum is changed by torque, following the relationship $\text{net}\;\ktau = \frac{\kdLang}{\kdt}$.
  • Angular momentum is conserved if the net torque is zero $\kL = \text{constant}\;(\text{net}\;\ktau = 0)$ or $\kL = \kLprime\;(\text{net}\;\ktau = 0)$. This equation is known as the law of conservation of angular momentum, which may be conserved in collisions.
notes: The two problems the book leaves unkeyed, the disk that arrives spinning at 1000 rpm and the person on ice who catches a ball with an outstretched arm, are left out along with the drawing of that catch, Figure 10.36.

Problems 2 (the disk spinning at 1000 rpm) and 4 (the person on ice catching a ball, which the CNXML leaves untyped and which is classed a problem by its header) have no keyed answer and are left out, and Figure 10.36 leaves with the fourth. Nothing is taken here from another section. Numeric answers accept 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: The bowling ball causes the pins to fly, some of them spinning violently. (credit: Tinou Bao, Flickr)

(a) A disk slides toward a motionless stick on a frictionless surface. (b) The disk hits the stick at one end and adheres to it, and they rotate together, pivoting around the nail. Angular momentum is conserved for this inelastic collision because the surface is frictionless and the unbalanced external force at the nail exerts no torque.

A disk hitting a stick is compared to a tennis ball being hit by a racquet. (a) When the ball strikes the racquet near the end, a backward force is exerted on the hand. (b) When the racquet is struck much farther down, a forward force is exerted on the hand. (c) When the racquet is struck at the percussion point, no force is delivered to the hand.

exercises.prompt: Is rotational kinetic energy a vector? Justify your answer.

answer.solution: No, energy is always scalar whether motion is involved or not. No form of energy has a direction in space and you can see that rotational kinetic energy does not depend on the direction of motion just as linear kinetic energy is independent of the direction of motion.

exercises.prompt: A box with a mass of 2.0 kg rests on one end of a seesaw. The seesaw is 6.0 m long, and we can assume it has negligible mass. Approximately what angular momentum will the box have if someone with a mass of 65 kg sits on the other end of the seesaw quickly, with a velocity of 1.2 m/s?

answer.hint: The person arriving at 1.2 m/s carries angular momentum about the pivot of $\kL = m\kv r$ with $r$ half the length of the seesaw, and the seesaw with the box on it takes that angular momentum up.

exercises.prompt: A spinner in a board game can be thought of as a thin rod that spins about an axis at its center. The spinner in a certain game is 12 cm long and has a mass of 10 g. How will its angular velocity change when it is flicked at one end with a force equivalent to 15 g travelling at 5.0 m/s if all the energy of the collision is transferred to the spinner? (You can use the table in Figure 10.12 to estimate the rotational inertia of the spinner.)

answer.solution: Take the flick to be a 15 g mass arriving at 5.0 m/s, so that its kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}m\kv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.015\ \text{kg})(5.0\ \text{m/s})^2 = 0.19\ \text{J}$. The question says that all of this energy goes into the spinner, so after the flick the spinner has rotational kinetic energy $\kKErot = \frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2 = 0.19\ \text{J}$. The spinner is a thin rod turning about its center, and Figure 10.12 gives $\kI = M\ell^2/12$ for that case, which with $M = 0.010\ \text{kg}$ and $\ell = 0.12\ \text{m}$ is $1.2 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$. Solving $\frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2 = 0.19\ \text{J}$ for $\kw$ then gives the angular velocity the spinner gains, which is on the order of $180\ \text{rad/s}$, from rest. Note that the question hands you energy rather than angular momentum; in the collision of the section the angular momentum is what is conserved and the kinetic energy is not, so this spinner is an idealization in which the flick loses nothing.

exercises.prompt: How could you use simple equipment such as balls and string to study the changes in angular momentum of a system when it interacts with another system?

answer.solution: Hang a ball on a string from a fixed point so that it can swing in a circle, and let a second ball, rolled along the floor or swung on a string of its own, strike it. Before the collision the moving ball has angular momentum about the fixed point equal to its mass times its speed times the perpendicular distance from the point to its path, as the disk in the section has $\kL = m\kv\kr$ about the nail. After the collision you can measure the angular velocity of whatever moves by timing its circling, and its moment of inertia is that of a point mass at the length of the string, so the angular momentum after can be compared with the angular momentum before. Vary how far from the fixed point the second ball strikes, whether the balls stick together or bounce apart, and whether the string is tied to a fixed point or held loosely, and record in each case whether the angular momentum of the two-ball system is the same before and after. The cases in which it is not are the cases in which the string or the support exerted a torque about the point you measured from.

exercises.prompt: Describe two different collisions—one in which angular momentum is conserved, and the other in which it is not. Which condition determines whether or not angular momentum is conserved in a collision?

answer.solution: Angular momentum is changed only by a net external torque, so the condition is whether the forces from outside the system have a lever arm about the point you take your angular momentum about. The disk and the nailed stick of this section are the first kind of collision: the nail pushes hard on the stick, but it pushes at the pivot, where its lever arm is zero, so it exerts no torque and the angular momentum of the disk and stick together is the same after the collision as before. For the second kind, let the same disk strike a stick that is held by a hand partway along its length, or let a ball strike a door that is being pushed shut at the same moment; the hand and the pusher act at a distance from the pivot, so they exert a torque during the collision and the angular momentum about the pivot changes. Note that the choice of point matters: a force that has no lever arm about one point has a lever arm about another, so the same collision can conserve angular momentum about the nail and not about the center of the stick.

exercises.prompt: Suppose an ice hockey puck strikes a hockey stick that lies flat on the ice and is free to move in any direction. Which quantities are likely to be conserved: angular momentum, linear momentum, or kinetic energy (assuming the puck and stick are very resilient)?

answer.solution: Ask of each quantity what could change it. Linear momentum is changed only by a net external force, and the ice is frictionless and the stick is not nailed down, so no external force acts along the ice and the linear momentum of the puck and stick together is conserved. Angular momentum is changed only by a net external torque, and with no external force there is no external torque either, so angular momentum is conserved as well, about any point you choose. Kinetic energy is the quantity that a collision can lose, as the disk and the stick of the section lose most of theirs when the disk sticks; but the question says the puck and stick are very resilient, which is to say the collision is nearly elastic, so kinetic energy is very nearly conserved too. All three are conserved here, and the stick that was nailed down in the section differs in the one respect that matters: its nail supplied the external force that changed the linear momentum of the system.

exercises.prompt: Repeat Example 10.15 in which the disk strikes and adheres to the stick 0.100 m from the nail.

parts.hint: The disk’s angular momentum about the nail is $m\kv\kr$ with $\kr = 0.100\ \text{m}$ now, and the moment of inertia after is $m\kr^2$ for the disk plus $M\ell^2/3$ for the whole 1.20 m stick.
The kinetic energy after the collision is $\frac{1}{2}\kIprime\kwprime^2$; the energy before is the disk’s 22.5 J as in the example.
After the collision the disk moves at $\kr\kwprime$ and the stick’s center of mass at $(\ell/2)\kwprime$, with $\ell$ the stick’s length rather than the distance to the strike.

exercises.prompt: Twin skaters approach one another as shown in Figure 10.35 and lock hands. (a) Calculate their final angular velocity, given each had an initial speed of 2.50 m/s relative to the ice. Each has a mass of 70.0 kg, and each has a center of mass located 0.800 m from their locked hands. You may approximate their moments of inertia to be that of point masses at this radius. (b) Compare the initial kinetic energy and final kinetic energy.

parts.hint: Each skater carries angular momentum $m\kv r$ about the locked hands, both in the same sense, and afterward the two turn together with a moment of inertia of two point masses at 0.800 m.
Compare the two skaters’ translational kinetic energy before with the rotational kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}\kI\kw^2$ of the pair after; the part asks for the final kinetic energy.

answer.solution: (a) 3.13 rad/s (b) Initial KE = 438 J, final KE = 438 J

exercises.prompt: Repeat Example 10.15 in which the stick is free to have translational motion as well as rotational motion.

parts.hint: With no nail there is no external force, so linear momentum is conserved as well as angular momentum, and the angular momentum is best taken about the center of mass of the disk and stick together, where the stick’s moment of inertia is $M\ell^2/12$.

The kinetic energy after is the translational kinetic energy of the center of mass plus the rotational kinetic energy about it; the part asks for the final kinetic energy, the initial being the disk’s 22.5 J.
Nothing external acts along the ice, so the linear momentum after is exactly the disk’s momentum before.

answer.solution: (a) 1.70 rad/s (b) Initial KE = 22.5 J, final KE = 2.04 J (c) $1.50\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$
